item.title: A Gaussian Process State Space Formulation for Materials Constitutive Modeling: Application to Quasi-brittle Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.33175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constitutive models for history-dependent, path-dependent materials typically encode this dependence in prescribed functional forms through internal variables such as damage or plastic strain that are phenomenological, model-dependent, and not directly observable. These rigid forms lack flexibility to match observations, make calibration potentially non-unique, and complicate uncertainty quantification. This paper develops a Gaussian-process state-space model (GP-SSM) that replaces the fixed form of the constitutive model with a flexible GP regression, and the prescribed internal variables with latent state variables learned directly from observable stress-strain histories. As a GP, the model is naturally endowed with a measure of uncertainty and can be constrained to satisfy physical principles. We demonstrate this framework for quasi-brittle materials under triaxial compression, where the latent variable evolution is driven by the current-state stress invariants and the increment of equivalent strain to reflect irreversible, pressure-sensitive history. A sparse multi-output GP then maps the latent state and current strain tensor to the six-component stress response, trained by variational sparse inference. The trained model is exported into Abaqus/Explicit through a user material subroutine. Four verification cases are reported: (1) offline rollout on validation and test histories; (2) a single element under changing confinement; (3) a frozen-memory unloading-reloading extension; and (4) a multi-element structural model compared against the Karagozian and Case Concrete (KCC) model. These results show that the learned state-space update reproduces held-out RVE-scale histories in closed-loop rollout, tracks evolving confinement, supports unloading without violating the irreversibility of the learned history state, and reproduces structural-level behavior consistent with KCC.
item.dc:creator: Houlin Xu, Chenyang Li, K. T. Ramesh, Michael D. Shields

item.title: A unified and composable framework for modeling packed-bed liquid chromatography
item.description: arXiv:2610.33269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Packed-bed chromatography is a cornerstone of bioseparation, yet its modeling landscape remains fragmented by numerous model variants, inconsistent terminology, and limited structural clarity. While prior work has categorized and contrasted individual variants, our approach shifts the focus to unification. We present a unified, modular, and composable framework that integrates diverse mechanistic packed-bed chromatography models into a coherent structure. Starting from a high-resolution three-dimensional model, the framework systematically derives a hierarchy of reduced-order models through formal model order reduction. It encompasses a broad range of bulk transport phenomena, intraparticle mass transfer processes, binding mechanisms, and chemical reactions. Formulated orthogonally, these modules are independently meaningful and can be systematically combined into mathematically consistent models tailored to specific applications. The framework recovers and generalizes existing models, establishes a consistent taxonomy, and enables novel model combinations and extensions, including alternative column and particle geometries, particle-size and particle-type distributions, component-specific pore accessibility, rapid-equilibrium binding and reaction formulations, and size-exclusion with simultaneous binding. The framework is accessible through CADET-Equations, an interactive web application for model assembly and automatic generation of governing equations in LaTeX, promoting standardization and transparency. Its design principles are increasingly reflected throughout the CADET ecosystem, whose modular architecture supports the majority of the proposed model family. The generality and composable design of the framework provide a foundation for extending chromatography modeling software toward integrated bioseparation processes and advanced computational biotechnology applications.
item.dc:creator: Jan Michael Breuer, Samuel Leweke, Johannes Schm\"older, Antonia Berger, Gregor J. Gassner, Eric von Lieres

item.title: Tokenised Sukuk: A Verifiable Architecture for Asset Evidence and Programmable Shariah Compliance
item.description: arXiv:2610.33538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security-token standards such as ERC-3643 decide who may hold a token, not what stands behind it. For a sukuk this gap matters: whether a certificate may trade at a negotiated price depends on what its portfolio contains, and a token that checks only investor identity keeps trading after every non-debt asset has been sold. We ask whether this tradability condition can be enforced on-chain, and at what cost. We encode the tradability conditions of the 2023 resolution of the Shariah Advisory Council of the Securities Commission Malaysia on Sukuk Wakalah bi al-Istithmar as issuance and transfer policies that read EIP-712 claims, signed by separate institutional roles, about each asset's rights, valuation, encumbrance and Shariah classification and about the allocation of proceeds. Across 26 scenarios that we constructed on a synthetic instrument, an identity-only baseline wrongly allowed 13 operations that the encoded policy denies, and asset evidence without the Shariah rule still allowed 6. The full policy matched every expected outcome and added 35,834 gas (71.0%) per transfer, independent of portfolio size. Our evaluation also exposes a trade-off that the constructed scenarios had missed. Checking the continuing condition through a single nominated asset keeps the cost of a transfer constant but can block trades the ruling allows, and a bounded fallback scan narrows this gap at about 12,050 gas per scanned asset. Our results indicate that Shariah tradability conditions can be enforced on-chain against attributable asset evidence, and that the way a ruling is encoded shapes which lawful trades a token permits. GitHub repo: https://github.com/rischanlab/tokenized_sukuk
item.dc:creator: Rischan Mafrur, Khadijah, Gun Gun Febrianza

item.title: Reliability Assessment of FRP-RC Columns Using AK-MCS with a Piecewise Two-Branch Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.34472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Slender concrete columns reinforced with fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) bars fail at medium to high axial load levels either by concrete crushing or by loss of stability, while the tensile strains in the reinforcement remain far below the rupture strain. Each non-linear finite element (FE) analysis yields only the capacity of the governing failure mode, and the governing mode changes over a broad zone in which both capacities are nearly equal. Both characteristics conflict with active-learning Kriging-assisted Monte Carlo simulation (AK-MCS), which assumes a single, smooth limit-state function. This paper proposes a piecewise, two-branch AK-MCS framework in which each failure mode is represented by its own Kriging model, trained only on the FE analyses in which that mode governs, and the governing prediction is the minimum of both. Safeguards against data starvation keep rarely governing branches usable. After convergence, additional FE analyses are placed based on a leave-one-out calibration check and on the width of the confidence interval on the reliability index. A design-point search on the surrogate and importance sampling at the design points provide the reliability index even where direct Monte Carlo simulation finds no failure. For an FRP-reinforced concrete column example with mixed failure, 79% and 62% of the training points lie near the mode boundary. The reliability index from the design-point search agrees with the Monte Carlo estimate to within 0.05, and an FE analysis at the design point confirms the surrogate to within 0.6%.
item.dc:creator: Arndt Goldack, Richard Koehler, Ahmed Usama Syed

item.title: A Product-Grassmann Tucker Surrogate for Parametric Field Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.34559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many-query applications such as design optimization, uncertainty quantification and digital twins call for repeated full-field predictions from expensive partial differential equation (PDE) simulations. Grassmannian reduced-order models interpolate parameter-dependent subspaces but commonly vectorize the spatial field, and the ambient dimension then grows with the product of the grid sizes. Tensor-based models preserve the multiway structure but often use shared mode-wise bases or a fixed core across parameters. We propose a Tucker-based surrogate that keeps the spatial directions and time as separate modes. The factor subspaces are interpolated on a product Grassmann manifold, Procrustes alignment places the Tucker cores in one coordinate system, and a truncated singular value decomposition models their variation. Across five PDE benchmarks in two and three spatial dimensions, including public computational fluid dynamics data, the interpolation size is reduced by factors of 13 to 482 and the stored model by factors of 13 to 464 relative to a single-subspace Grassmannian surrogate with the same local interpolation. Cached queries run 3.3 to 8.5 times faster, the mean errors over ten resampled splits differ by at most 0.22 percentage points (0.36 when every model choice is re-selected inside each split), and the prediction-error terms of the two methods differ by less than 0.1 percentage points. The remaining accuracy differences are consistent with the larger representation error of the Tucker format. In a three-dimensional grid study the interpolation-size ratio rises to 2,260 and the query speedup to 11.9 at 64^3.
item.dc:creator: Melika Baghi, Xiao Liu, Kamran Paynabar

item.title: Constrained neural softening functions for the Mullins effect in parameter-dependent materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.34565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurately capturing the Mullins effect across varying material compositions remains challenging, as constitutive models must unify flexible representations of stress softening with physical consistency and robust parameter calibration. In this work, we investigate parameter-dependent physics-augmented neural network constitutive models within the pseudo-elastic modeling framework, focusing on structural constraints that ensure physically admissible neural softening functions. This paper has three key contributions: (1) We formulate different neural softening functions within the pseudo-elastic framework, including a multiplicative decomposition of the softening function that enables parameter-dependent ansatz functions satisfying common mechanical constitutive conditions by construction. (2) We derive a sufficient condition for ellipticity of pseudo-elastic constitutive models, which can be enforced in the constitutive models by construction. (3) We systematically investigate how flexibility and structural constraints influence the performance of neural softening functions in terms of prediction accuracy and calibration robustness. For this, we consider multiaxial experimental data of carbon black-filled EPDM rubber synthesized with varying amounts of curatives. The findings of our work suggest that neural softening functions are a promising extension of the classical pseudo-elastic framework and, when subject to suitable constraints, can improve predictive accuracy for highly nonlinear, parameter-dependent materials.
item.dc:creator: Dominik K. Klein, Jonas Fey, Maximilian Kannapinn, Oliver Weeger

item.title: Faster Polyhedral Intersections in 3D
item.description: arXiv:2610.34702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The operation of intersecting two polyhedra, which can be reduced to clipping one polyhedron with a series of planes formed from another polyhedron, is central to intersection based mesh interpolation and material interface reconstruction. R3D is a robust library for such operation which implements the algorithm of Sugihara. In this paper, we present J3D, a new implementation of the clipping algorithm of Sugihara that provides substantial performance improvements over R3D.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Donato, Daniel Shevitz, Rao Garimella

item.title: Beyond Profit Rankings: Identifying, Understanding, and Evaluating Smart Money in Prediction Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.34754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prediction markets have emerged as an important mechanism for aggregating information and trading beliefs about future events. The transparency of on-chain transactions has enabled investors to identify historically profitable wallets, commonly referred to as smart money, and replicate their trading activities through copy trading. However, despite the growing popularity of smart-money tracking, systematic research on these wallets' trading behavior, profitability persistence, and the economic feasibility of following their trades remains limited. To address this gap, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study of Polymarket, the most popular decentralized prediction market, by reconstructing wallet-level trading activities from on-chain transactions, position changes, market histories, and settlement outcomes. We first examine the distribution and persistence of historical profitability using statistical analysis and logistic regression, and further characterize heterogeneous trading strategies through multidimensional behavioral profiling and unsupervised clustering. Building on these findings, we develop an evidence-grounded multi-agent research framework that integrates wallet behavior, market conditions, and real-world information to generate interpretable and verifiable explanations of individual trades. Finally, we implement a real-time copy-trading system and evaluate its practical feasibility through order-book-aware paper trading and live on-chain execution. Our findings reveal substantial behavioral heterogeneity among historically profitable wallets and highlight the challenges of translating observed trading performance into replicable economic returns.
item.dc:creator: Huaiyu Jia, Shuo Sun

item.title: A Multi-Asset Dataset and Tail-Risk Framework for DeFi Yield Trading Derivatives
item.description: arXiv:2610.34930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Yield trading has emerged as a pivotal innovation in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) by decoupling principal from yield streams to enhance capital efficiency. Despite its significance, the field lacks fine-grained datasets for systematic empirical analysis. We address this gap by constructing the first large-scale benchmark dataset for Pendle, the pioneering on-chain interest rate derivatives protocol, spanning 24 months across 340 active markets with complete lifecycle observations. Our analysis reveals a structural market transition toward stablecoin-dominated "flight-to-quality" dynamics. To tackle the heavy-tailed nature of yield data, we propose Tail-MSE, an asymmetric loss function that prioritizes tail risk awareness through dynamic penalty weighting. Experiments across six state-of-the-art time series models demonstrate consistent improvements in volatility forecasting robustness, enabling the Tail-MSE Sniper strategy to achieve superior risk-adjusted returns in over half of all markets.
item.dc:creator: Huaiyu Jia, Jieshun You, Jingyu Liu, Yizhi Luo, Shuo Sun

item.title: Consequence-guided clarification: releasing minimum-compliance topology-optimized designs from incomplete specifications
item.description: arXiv:2610.34957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A converged topology optimization can solve the wrong problem when loads, supports, or the domain are underspecified. Assuming defaults, or asking the problem's author about every detail, ignores how much each answer changes the design. We propose consequence-guided clarification (CGC), which bases acceptance on computed mechanical consequences. CGC computes a reference design for each of a finite list of complete specifications, called readings. A design is accepted only if its compliance is at most 5% above the reference at every reading consistent with the answers. Otherwise, CGC asks the question whose worst answer leaves the smallest worst-case excess, and withholds acceptance at its question limit. To save optimizations, the screening variant CGC-S postpones some references until a candidate must be checked. We developed and evaluated both on 36 arXiv-derived tasks, treating each of 134 readings in turn as intended and simulating correct answers. In 26 tasks, the default-reading design failed another reading. Apart from always-asked questions on load direction, sign, and material budget, asking everything took 188 questions; CGC and CGC-S each took 105. The acceptance test supplied most of this saving: applying it to the default design alone took 117. Relative to asking everything, CGC-S requested 4.6 extra reference designs per avoided question, each from two optimization starts, counting optimization time only. References are not certified optima: better ones pushed three accepted cases above tolerance, and finer meshes changed some decisions. Within these limits, the test shows which readings a design covers and which details block acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Shaoliang Yang, Jun Wang

item.title: MarkovSim: an LLM Agent Harness with Bounded Context for Long-Horizon Computational Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies have applied large language model (LLM) agent systems to computational simulation workflows. Such workflows are long-horizon, so the information generated can exceed what an LLM can reason over at once, its context window. Context management is therefore essential, yet existing systems have either neglected it or treated it as a supporting mechanism rather than a subject of study. This paper presents MarkovSim, an LLM agent harness for long-horizon computational simulation, whose core is a context management scheme built into the workflow. The workflow record is written to a memory system with a predefined schema, and at workflow-defined boundaries, namely the state transitions of a finite-state machine a compact representation of the solution progress is constructed from it as the agent's context. Instantiated on finite element analysis and evaluated on six benchmark problems, MarkovSim passed 16 of 18 runs and corrected its own faults in both the solver operations and the model physics. The engineer was consulted only where engineering judgement was needed. The context remained bounded throughout every run, regardless of its length.
item.dc:creator: Yeui-Lung Lei, Wen-Bo Chen, Pan Zhang

item.title: Multi-Fidelity Particle Flow Filters based on Log Homotopy
item.description: arXiv:2610.35712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work proposes a new Multi-Fidelity Particle Flow Filter (MFPFF) based on a linear control variate framework and multilevel Monte Carlo methods. Conventional particle filters often suffer from weight collapse and particle degeneracy in high-dimensional spaces. Particle flow filters address this by smoothly transporting prior particles toward the posterior distribution, thereby avoiding the need for resampling. This work constructs multi-fidelity particle flow filters by augmenting a small number of expensive high-fidelity particles (full-order model runs) with a large number of inexpensive low-resolution particles (reduced-order surrogates constructed via intrusive Galerkin projection). These surrogates act as control variates to enhance the statistical estimate of the full-order posterior, yielding enhanced analysis accuracy at comparable computational cost. The work focuses on two particle flows based on log homotopy, the stochastic Gromov flow and deterministic Exact flow. Numerical experiments with the Korteweg-De Vries (KdV) and Quasi-Geostrophic (QG) test problems demonstrate that the proposed MFPFF achieves accuracy comparable to high-fidelity simulations while significantly reducing computational expense.
item.dc:creator: Abhinab Bhattacharjee, Andrey A. Popov, Amit N. Subrahmanya, Adrian Sandu

item.title: EL-DIP: A Deep Image Prior Framework for Accurate,Efficient, and Noise-Robust Elastography
item.description: arXiv:2610.33091v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Elastography is a key technique for non-invasive imaging, yet it remains severely ill-posed and sensitive to measurement noise, causing blurring and artifacts. We propose EL-DIP, a training-data-free framework based on deep image prior (DIP) that reconstructs heterogeneous shear modulus distributions. Inverse distance weighting interpolation enables arbitrary-shaped domains, and adjoint sensitivity analysis provides efficient gradient computation. Numerical and experimental studies show that EL-DIP accurately recovers inclusion geometry and modulus across different noise levels. Under extreme noise, image fidelity improves by approximately 97.1% over conventional methods. We believe that this method has great potential as a robust tool for biomedical diagnosis,biomechanical characterization, and non-destructive evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Hao Liu, Fuyi Li, Dong Liu, Yue Mei, Sheng Mao

item.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mechanical Engineering: Foundations, Opportunities, Challenges, and Responsibilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.33105v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping mechanical engineering (ME), from modeling, simulation, and optimization to diagnostics, design, and technical communication. Drawing on a round-table at the 28th ABCM International Congress on Mechanical Engineering (COBEM 2025), this article presents a structured perspective for the Brazilian and international ME communities. Rather than an exhaustive survey, it examines how AI can enhance engineering practice without compromising scientific rigor. We distinguish statistical learning from human cognition and discuss the capabilities, limitations, and emerging agentic forms of AI. We then consider industrial adoption, workforce changes, and AI-assisted scientific discovery, alongside the energy and infrastructure demands of AI computation and their implications for sustainability and thermal management. The discussion emphasizes the integration of physical knowledge, structured reasoning, and domain expertise into AI systems, particularly in safety-relevant applications. Topics include physics-informed and hybrid learning, physically constrained modeling, validation, uncertainty quantification, and certification. We also examine educational, epistemological, and ethical challenges, including curriculum reform, human-agent collaboration, professional accountability, and the preservation of engineering knowledge. We conclude with principles for responsible AI adoption in ME: physical consistency, rigorous validation, explicit treatment of uncertainty, energy sustainability, human oversight, and ethical responsibility. AI should complement, not replace, engineering judgment.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: J. Braz. Soc. Mech. Sci. Eng. 48, 741 (2026)
item.dc:creator: A. Cunha Jr, C. Nataraj, L. M. Lorenzo, H. Panetto, A. Scotti, J. V. C. Vargas

item.title: Modeling Liquid-Cooled Data Centers in EnergyPlus
item.description: arXiv:2610.33148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As AI workloads accelerate data center transition toward high-density racks with direct-to-chip (DTC) liquid cooling, existing simulation tools remain limited in evaluating whole-building and multi-year efficiency. To bridge this gap, we develop a native EnergyPlus object, ElectricEquipment:ITE:LiquidCooled, that models DTC liquid cooling for chilled-water and warm-water architectures as plant-loop components. It couples facility-water loops, rack-side secondary loops, coolant distribution units, and chip-junction temperatures within a single solver. Validation against an independent Modelica implementation across 21 operating conditions, including two full-year runs compared at one-minute resolution, yields loop-temperature RMSE at or below 0.021 K, well within the 0.1 K acceptance threshold. Our case study demonstrates that warm-water liquid cooling reduces annual PUE from 1.43 to 1.25, eliminates on-site water use, and cuts total facility energy by 37.9% relative to an air-cooled baseline. By embedding liquid-cooling logic into EnergyPlus, our work provides whole-building, long-term energy modeling for high-density AI infrastructure within an open-source framework.
item.dc:creator: Yun-Dam Ko, Dipashreya A. Sur, Cade Napier, Carlos D. D\'iaz-Mar\'in, Rishee K. Jain

item.title: Two Uncertainties Are Not One: Disagreement versus Decision-Risk in Cheap Structured Content Moderation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Content moderation compresses a graded, contested human judgment into a binary act (leave up / take down) over billions of items, at a scale where running a frontier LLM on every post is uneconomical. A new class of frozen "System One" models returns typed, calibrated decisions instead of text at ~USD 0.000025 per call and ~100 ms. We run the first independent audit of one such model on 142,658 human-labeled comments, and benchmark it against 14 frontier reasoning models (the GPT-5.x, Claude, Gemini 3, and Grok families) on a shared probe set. Two findings stand out. First, the cheap model is accuracy-competitive: its zero-shot classification AUROC (0.83) is not statistically separable (paired bootstrap, n=56; a failure to reject parity, not proof of equivalence) from 13 of the 14 frontier systems while costing 1-3 orders of magnitude less, and it is no worse calibrated than several of them. Second, "confidence" conflates two uncertainties that come apart: human disagreement (where annotators split on satire and coded language) and decision risk (where the automatic action is costly-wrong). Under an asymmetric moderation loss these call for opposite escalation signals, so no single confidence number serves both. Because the model prices extra questions at nearly zero, decomposing the judgment into parallel sub-questions and reading their spread recovers a human-disagreement signal that the model's native confidence misses -- but this remedy is specific: it helps the weakest, disagreement-blind models and only when the decomposition aligns with the sources of disagreement; a specialist toxicity model and the strongest LLMs do not need it, and the effect is distribution-sensitive. We will release the instrument, the cached runs, and the analysis.
item.dc:creator: Karan Yadav

item.title: From Hype to ROI: An Economic Model for LLM Adoption in Information Systems and Security Operations
item.description: arXiv:2610.33352v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) promise significant efficiency gains across information-intensive operations by automating repetitive language-based tasks. However, adoption decisions remain largely opportunistic, as organizations struggle to move from pilots to sustainable industrialization. Without systematic economic frameworks, practitioners cannot assess whether LLM investments create value in a given context. This paper develops a general economic model to support informed LLM adoption decisions in operational information systems. Facing high uncertainty, we represent parameters as random variables centered on authoritative benchmarks, and evaluate the model by Monte Carlo simulation across pessimistic-to-optimistic assumptions on LLM efficiency. The ROI distributions show the probability of profitability and the Value at Risk for each configuration, together with a sensitivity analysis of its main drivers. As a first instantiation, we apply the model to Security Operations Centers (SOCs), mapping workflows onto established standards to identify tasks suited to LLM augmentation. The model balances productivity gains, driven by alert volume, analyst effort, and LLM efficiency, against operational costs, including inference, infrastructure, and error remediation, covering both cloud API and self-hosted deployments. Results show that adoption economics are context-dependent, and that automation is an exploitable lever, gated by accuracy, while the cost of errors and the model's price are secondary. Across the analyzed models and prices, most configurations are unprofitable, with profitability limited to high-accuracy, low-uncertainty deployments. The model gives organizations a quantitative basis for evidence-based adoption decisions, by locating the boundary between profit and loss, and the loss risked beyond it.
item.dc:creator: Pellegrino Casoria, Andrea Araldo, Rosario Patan\`e, Simon Pietro Romano

item.title: A Differentiable Framework for Inverse Identification of Heterogeneous Cohesive Laws
item.description: arXiv:2610.33711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work develops a differentiable finite element framework based on an intrinsic cohesive-zone formulation for identifying traction-separation laws from global force-displacement histories and spatially sparse strain measurements. The framework employs physics-constrained neural networks to represent flexible, thermodynamically structured cohesive laws, with sensitivities computed through automatic differentiation and a discrete adjoint that accounts for the history-dependent evolution of interfacial damage. To enable identification of spatially heterogeneous cohesive behavior, we extend learned constitutive priors to irreversible interfacial damage by constructing a shared, low-dimensional family of cohesive laws from representative traction-separation histories. This representation exploits common constitutive structure and parameter sharing to reduce the number of unknowns and regularize the inverse problem, while allowing local cohesive behavior to vary spatially through latent coordinates. Numerical investigations involving double-cantilever beams and fiber-matrix composites demonstrate that accurate reproduction of global force-displacement responses does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of the underlying cohesive laws. Incorporating spatially resolved strain measurements substantially improves constitutive identification, even when the admissible responses are constrained by a learned prior. Comparisons with conventional bilinear cohesive models and Bayesian optimization further illustrate the benefits of the learned constitutive representation and adjoint-based identification for high-dimensional inverse problems.
item.dc:creator: Sida Hao, Jinkyo Han, Bahador Bahmani

item.title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for PHM: What Transfers, What Does Not, and What Federating It Costs
item.description: arXiv:2610.35280v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has produced capable time-series foundation models, but its value for Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) has not been measured under leakage-controlled conditions. We measure it on a corpus of 47 public PHM datasets, harmonized to a single tensor contract and partitioned so that 11 datasets are withheld from pretraining in full. Transfer turns out to be task-dependent: a compact channel-independent Transformer encoder (801,808 parameters) pretrained with masked patch prediction raises fault-classification macro-F1 from 0.350 to 0.812 on CWRU and from 0.569 to 0.951 on HSG18, yet on CMAPSS remaining-useful-life estimation no pretrained checkpoint reliably improves upon a from-scratch baseline. We pretrain under two regimes---centralized, and simulated cross-silo federated with ten clients grouped by physical domain---holding architecture, objective, source data and optimization budget fixed. Two further findings are negative. At matched budget the centralized encoder leads by 15.5--20.2 macro-F1 points in four of four comparisons, although the comparison is confounded by a learning-rate schedule that favours the centralized arm and rests on a single pretraining run per regime; on RUL the two regimes are indistinguishable. And the intrinsic SSL loss is not a valid selection criterion: the centralized encoder more than halves the federated reconstruction loss without a corresponding gap on RUL, and a server-momentum sweep moves downstream validation macro-F1 by up to 0.29 while the SSL loss varies by 0.021. Transfer also hinges on the backbone learning rate: the same checkpoint yields 0.169 or 0.829 macro-F1 on CWRU depending on a single order of magnitude. We release the corpus pipeline, the protocol and the code.
item.dc:creator: Jos\'e Sanz-Dur\'an, David Sol\'is-Mart\'in

item.title: Differentiable FEM versus PINN for pavement layer inverse analysis: enforcing physics as hard or soft constraints
item.description: arXiv:2606.03210v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automatic-differentiation-based inverse analysis methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and differentiable programming, have recently shown great promise due to their ability to compute accurate gradients and convergence efficiency. However, their applicability to falling weight deflectometer (FWD) backcalculation remains unexplored. This study critically evaluates PINN-based inverse analysis for a multilayer pavement system and investigates differentiable finite element method (DiffFEM) as an alternative based on a synthetic benchmark. The standard PINN does not recover layer moduli because of the sharp domain discontinuities inherent to layered pavement systems. Although we use an extended PINN with domain decomposition (XPINN), which shows better performance on discontinuous domains, its performance remains highly sensitive to loss weighting and network architecture, and degrades under measurement noise. By contrast, DiffFEM consistently achieves more accurate, stable, and computationally efficient inversion results. These results show and quantify the expected advantage of DiffFEM, which enforces the governing physics as a hard constraint in the solver, over PINN-based approaches, where the governing physics is imposed as a soft constraint through the loss function. More broadly, the findings suggest that the choice between PINN- and DiffFEM-based inverse analysis needs careful consideration, with DiffFEM offering practical advantages when an efficient and robust differentiable forward solver is available.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Computer-Aided Civil and Infrastructure Engineering, Vol. 51, 100251 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Yongjin Choi, Hyeonbin Moon, Seunghwa Ryu

item.title: Bayesian Variational System Identification with Weak-Form Residual Likelihoods
item.description: arXiv:2606.14942v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider system identification for discovering parameterized operators in governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from noisy spatiotemporal data. Building on variational system identification (VSI), which identifies PDEs through Galerkin weak-form residuals, we develop a Bayesian VSI (B-VSI) framework for operator selection, parameter estimation, and uncertainty quantification. The central idea is to define the likelihood directly in weak-form residual space by propagating observation uncertainty through the weak-form residual map. The resulting likelihood captures heteroscedastic and correlated residual errors while avoiding repeated forward PDE solves during inference. For efficient computation, we use lagged-covariance updates that yield generalized least-squares estimates and conjugate posterior approximations when applicable, together with gradient-based and particle-based methods for more general priors and posterior structures. Model-form uncertainty is handled through sequential operator elimination guided by a residual-space Bayesian information criterion. We demonstrate the framework on state-linear and nonlinear PDEs, including the Fokker--Planck equation and a two-field Cahn--Hilliard equation. The results show that B-VSI accurately recovers active operators and coefficients from noisy data, improves robustness relative to classical VSI, and provides posterior uncertainty estimates for coefficients and derived physical quantities.
item.dc:creator: Chengyang Huang, Siddhartha Srivastava, Krishna Garikipati, Xun Huan

item.title: Refined Thompson Learning for Adaptive Bandits: Power-Efficient Flexibility Scheduling Across Data Centers
item.description: arXiv:2608.00921v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid growth of large-scale AI workloads in data centers has placed increasing pressure on power grids in recent years. Since power systems must continuously balance supply and demand, there is growing interest in leveraging data-center workload flexibility as a grid service. We propose a contextual restless multi-armed bandit (CRMAB) framework in which a grid operator requests load reductions without observing internal job-scheduling decisions. Under an index-ability guarantee, each data center or physical machine is modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP) over a cyclic virtual-machine (VM) job queue, with unknown rewards and transition dynamics that are learned online using Thompson sampling and Whittle-index policies. To improve learning under sparse and noisy observations, the framework augments an adaptive Thompson--Whittle (TW) policy with domain-informed transition priors and gated prior mixing. In baseline experiments, the best refined adaptive variant achieves 91.4\% of the oracle reward after 100 rounds and 96.8\% after 1,000 rounds. Across a 16-setting stress test spanning different state-space sizes and levels of contextual feature noise, the best refined variant consistently outperforms the original TW policy with high confidence while remaining competitive with EXP4. A graph-based prior further incorporates data-center hardware constraints, including operating frequency and computing-resource limits. Overall, our results demonstrate the economic potential of data-center flexibility as a grid service and highlight the importance of high-quality, open-source AI workload traces for developing and evaluating such services.
item.dc:creator: Yifu Ding, Zixi Chen, Ruicheng Ao, David Simchi-Levi, Thomas Magnanti

item.title: VeriFin: A Neurosymbolic Framework for Verifying LLM-Generated Financial Claims
item.description: arXiv:2608.10213v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being adopted in financial workflows, where accuracy and reliability are critical. One such application is financial question answering over public company filings. However, LLMs struggle with quantitative financial reasoning, including identifying financial facts, interpreting reporting periods and units, and determining appropriate metrics, leading to incorrect answers. Recent RAG-based methods have improved financial question answering but do not ensure factual and numerical correctness. LLM-based verifiers may also accept incorrect numerical claims. To address this, we introduce VeriFin, a neurosymbolic framework for verifying LLM generated numerical financial claims. Given a question and a generated answer, VeriFin retrieves filing evidence, grounds values in XBRL facts, and establishes the required formula independently of the answer. It then uses the Z3 SMT solver to check the resulting arithmetic constraints. VeriFin accepts consistent claims, rejects inconsistent claims, and abstains when required facts or formulas cannot be established. To evaluate VeriFin, we constructed XBRLFiling, a dataset of 600 numerical questions from corporate filings, and selected 67 and 403 questions from FinanceBench and TAT-DQA, respectively. Across six answer models and three datasets, VeriFin achieves 100% observed precision among accepted answers with known correctness. For Qwen3-30B on XBRLFiling, VeriFin accepts 304 correct answers compared to 166 for an LLM judge, while reducing false accepts from 87 to 0. We release our benchmark to support research on reliable financial question answering.
item.dc:creator: Bethel Hall, Sachi Shome, William Eiers

item.title: Multimaterial topology optimization using SIMP, DMO and gSF: A comparative study with honeycomb tessellations
item.description: arXiv:2609.25976v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a comparative study of multimaterial topology optimization (MMTO) using the extended SIMP, Discrete Material Optimization (DMO), and generalized shape functions (gSF) approaches. The computational domain is discretized into hexagonal cells. Each cell is connected to its neighbors with edges. This characteristic reduces mesh-related effects on the optimized designs compared with conventional triangular and quadrilateral discretizations. Structural compliance is minimized at the prescribed volume fractions. The method of moving asymptotes is employed to update the design variables. The resulting optimized topologies are compared in terms of material distribution, structural performance, convergence behavior, and the characteristics of the obtained material interfaces. The comparative investigation provides insights into the working principles and performance of the extended SIMP, DMO, and gSF interpolation schemes for MMTO.
item.dc:creator: Bhargav kumar Duru, Prabhat Kumar

item.title: A Topology-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Multi-Target Active Debris Removal using Gaussian Boson Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.31824v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The continued growth of orbital debris threatens the safety and sustainability of near-Earth space, making Active Debris Removal (ADR) an important mitigation strategy. Selecting $k$ targets from $N$ candidates yields a combinatorial search space of size $\binom{N}{k}$, making joint target selection and mission sequencing computationally demanding. We present a topology-aware quantum-classical framework integrating orbital mechanics, weighted orbital-transfer graphs, Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS), and multi-objective evolutionary optimization. Seven target-prioritization strategies represent physical consequence, orbital persistence, conjunction risk, network centrality, community structure, inferred source families, and random selection. GBS generates candidate target subsets from the weighted graph, which are then evaluated using PyGMO-based evolutionary optimization to identify servicing sequences that jointly minimize total velocity increment ($\Delta v$) and mission duration, accounting for modeled timing, propulsion, and mass feasibility. We evaluate the framework across three benchmark environments, SOCRATES Minefield, Collision Cloud, and Random, with candidate-pool sizes $N\in\{15,18,22,25\}$ and target cardinalities $k\in\{3,5\}$. The experiments characterize how benchmark topology, prioritization strategy, and problem scale relate to sampling behavior and downstream mission performance. By separating candidate-subset generation from detailed trajectory optimization, the framework offers a topology-aware approach to focusing computational effort on a limited set of candidate ADR missions.
item.dc:creator: Komal Pandya, Saiyam Sakhuja, Nagaraj Kattaian

item.title: Analytical benchmark problems and methodological framework for the assessment and comparison of multifidelity optimization methods
item.description: arXiv:2204.07867v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper introduces a comprehensive benchmarking framework that includes: (i) a suite of analytical benchmark optimization problems designed to stress-test and validate multifidelity methods; (ii) a set of assessment metrics for quantifying and comparing performance over measurable objectives; and (iii) the classification, evaluation, and comparison of several families of multifidelity optimization methods and frameworks using the proposed benchmarks to identify their respective strengths and weaknesses in real-world scenarios. The proposed benchmark problems are analytically defined functions carefully selected to capture mathematical challenges commonly encountered in real-world applications, including high dimensionality, multimodality, discontinuities, and noise. Their closed-form nature ensures computational efficiency, high reproducibility, and a clear separation of algorithmic behavior from numerical artifacts. The accompanying performance metrics support the systematic evaluation of multifidelity methods, measuring both optimization effectiveness and global approximation accuracy. By providing a rigorous, reproducible, and accessible benchmarking framework, this work aims to enable the broader community to understand, compare, and advance multifidelity optimization methods for complex problems in science and engineering.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Mainini, L., Serani, A., Pehlivan-Solak, H. et al. Analytical benchmark problems and methodological framework for the assessment and comparison of multifidelity optimization methods. Arch Computat Methods Eng 33, 2969-3000 (2026)

item.title: Graph Neural Networks for Supply Chain Management: A Framework and Real World Benchmark
item.description: arXiv:2411.08550v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently gained traction in transportation, bioinformatics, language and image processing, but research on their application to supply chain management remains limited. Supply chains are inherently graph-like, making them ideal for GNN methodologies, which can optimize and solve complex problems. The barriers include a lack of proper conceptual foundations, familiarity with graph applications in SCM, and real-world benchmark datasets for GNN-based supply chain research. To address this, we discuss and connect supply chains with graph structures for effective GNN application, providing detailed formulations, examples, mathematical definitions, and task guidelines. Additionally, we present a multi-perspective real-world benchmark dataset from a leading FMCG company in Bangladesh, focusing on supply chain planning. We discuss various supply chain tasks using GNNs and benchmark several state-of-the-art models on homogeneous and heterogeneous graphs across six supply chain analytics tasks. Our analysis shows that GNN-based models consistently outperform statistical Machine Learning and other Deep Learning models by around 10-30% in regression, 10-30% in classification and detection tasks, and 15-40% in anomaly detection tasks on designated metrics. With this work, we lay the groundwork for solving supply chain problems using GNNs, supported by conceptual discussions, methodological insights, and a comprehensive dataset.
item.dc:creator: Azmine Toushik Wasi, MD Shafikul Islam

item.title: Fair Dynamic Operating Envelopes using Distributed Multi-Period Optimal Power Flow and Jain Index for Active Distribution Networks
item.description: arXiv:2608.23444v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dynamic operating envelopes (DOEs) are increasingly used to publish time-varying export limits that keep distribution networks within operational limits. Purely technical DOE allocation, however, can systematically privilege electrically favorable prosumers, while embedding fairness directly into a single-period optimal power flow (OPF) objective mixes network feasibility, equity and efficiency in a way that obscures the cost of fairness. This paper proposes a two-stage, multi-period framework that addresses both of these. Initially, a technical distributed OPF computes network-feasible export envelopes. The subsequent stage then applies a dynamic aggregate export budget and redistributes capacity through cumulative proportional fairness, limiting the additional curtailment by an admissible efficiency budget. The resulting fair DOEs are treated as first-stage decisions, while battery storage provides scenario-dependent recourse under demand and renewable uncertainty. The operational problem is solved by a calibrated regional alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) on a lossless LinDistFlow model and independently validated using AC power flow. We observe a trade-off between increases in curtailment \emph{versus} improvements on fairness, as expected, reaching Jain fairness indices close to unity. Results show that considering both storage (which alleviates curtailment impact) and multi-period fairness (which increases curtailment) is an interesting approach for modern DOE design, which in turn requires a multi-period, co-designed approach.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Salom\~ao Quessongo, Daniel Gebbran, Clodomiro Unsihuay-Vila
